<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:lms}
  For every integer $k\ge2$ and every real $0\le x\le1/k$,
  \[
    \Phi_k(x)=\max\{1-(1-x)^k,(kx)^k\}.
  \]
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:iid-tail}
  For every integer $k\ge1$ and every real $x\ge0$,
  \[
    \Phi_k(x)=
    \begin{cases}
      \max\{1-(1-x)^k,(kx)^k\}, & 0\le x\le1/k, \\
      1,                        & x\ge1/k.
    \end{cases}
  \]
  The maximizing distributions are characterized as follows.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item For $k=1$ and $0\le x\le1$, the unique maximizing distribution is $\mathsf B_x$.
    \item For $k\ge2$ and $0\le x<\beta_k$, the unique maximizing distribution is $\mathsf B_x$.
    \item For $k\ge2$ and $x=\beta_k$, the maximizing distributions are exactly $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ and $\mathsf C_{k,\beta_k}$.
    \item For $k\ge2$ and $\beta_k<x\le1/k$, the unique maximizing distribution is $\mathsf C_{k,x}$.
    \item For every $k\ge1$ and $x>1/k$, a distribution with mean at most $x$ is maximizing if and only if it assigns probability one to $[1/k,\infty)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
\label{conj:emc}
  Let $n,k,s$ be positive integers with $n\ge k(s+1)$.
  If $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ and $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s$, then $|\mathcal F|\le\max\{C_k(s),M_k(n,s)\}$.
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:emc}
    For every fixed integer $k\ge3$, there is an integer $s_{\mathrm{EMC}}(k)$ such that, for all integers $s\ge s_{\mathrm{EMC}}(k)$ and $n\ge k(s+1)$, every family $\mathcal F\subseteq\binom{[n]}k$ with $\nu(\mathcal F)\le s$ satisfies
    \[
      |\mathcal F|\le\max\{C_k(s),M_k(n,s)\}.
    \]
    The equality cases are as follows.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
      \item If $M_k(n,s)>C_k(s)$, then equality holds if and only if $\mathcal F=\mathcal A(S)$ for some $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$.
      \item If $M_k(n,s)<C_k(s)$, then equality holds if and only if $\mathcal F=\binom Qk$ for some $(k(s+1)-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$.
      \item If $M_k(n,s)=C_k(s)$, then equality holds if and only if $\mathcal F=\mathcal A(S)$ for some $s$-set $S\subseteq[n]$ or $\mathcal F=\binom Qk$ for some $(k(s+1)-1)$-set $Q\subseteq[n]$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:dimension-one}
  For every $x\ge0$, we have $\Phi_1(x)=\min\{x,1\}$.
  For $0\le x\le1$, the unique maximizing law is $\mathsf B_x=(1-x)\delta_0+x\delta_1$.
  For $x>1$, a probability law on $[0,\infty)$ with mean at most $x$ is maximizing if and only if it is supported on $[1,\infty)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $0\le x\le1$, and let $X$ be a nonnegative random variable with $\mathbb{E} X\le x$.
  Markov's inequality yields
  \[
    \mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=\mathbb{E}\1_{\{X\ge1\}}\le\mathbb{E} X\le x.
  \]
  The law $\mathsf B_x$ has mean $x$ and success probability $x$, so $\Phi_1(x)=x$.

  If $\mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=x$, then $\mathbb{E} X=\mathbb{E}\1_{\{X\ge1\}}=x$, so the nonnegative random variable $X-\1_{\{X\ge1\}}$ has expectation zero and hence vanishes almost surely.
  Thus, $X$ takes only the values zero and one, with $\mathbb{P}(X=1)=x$, so its law is $\mathsf B_x$.

  For $x>1$, the law $\delta_1$ is feasible and has success probability one, so $\Phi_1(x)=1$.
  For any nonnegative random variable $X$ with $\mathbb{E} X\le x$, its law attains this value exactly when $\mathbb{P}(X\ge1)=1$, which is equivalent to being supported on $[1,\infty)$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:crossing-parameters}
    For every integer $k\ge2$, the equation $g_k(c)=1$ has a unique solution $c=c_k$ in $[0,\infty)$, and ${\beta_k}$ is the unique solution of $1-(1-x)^k=(kx)^k$ in $(0,1/k]$.
    Moreover, $c_2=1/2$ and $0<c_k<1/2$ for $k\ge3$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Differentiating \eqref{eq:sec3-crossing-function}, we obtain $g_k'(c)=(1+c/k)^{k-1}-(1+(c-1)/k)^{k-1}>0$ for $c\ge0$, so $g_k$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$.
    We have $g_k(0)=1-(1-1/k)^k<1$ and $g_k(1)=(1+1/k)^k-1>1$.
    Hence, there is a unique $c_k\in(0,1)$ satisfying $g_k(c_k)=1$.
    Multiplying $g_k(c_k)=1$ by $(k/(k+c_k))^k$, we obtain $1-(1-{\beta_k})^k=(k{\beta_k})^k$.
    The substitution $c=1/x-k$ is a bijection from $(0,1/k]$ to $[0,\infty)$ and transforms $1-(1-x)^k=(kx)^k$ into $g_k(c)=1$.
            Since $g_k(c)=1$ has the unique solution $c=c_k$, the equation $1-(1-x)^k=(kx)^k$ has the unique solution $x=1/(k+c_k)=\beta_k$ in $(0,1/k]$.
    For $k=2$, the equation $g_2(c)=1$ has the unique solution $c_2=1/2$, and the corresponding crossing mean is $\beta_2=2/5$.
    For $k\ge3$,
      \[
        \left(1+\frac1{2k}\right)^k-\left(1-\frac1{2k}\right)^k
        =1+2\sum_{\substack{3\le j\le k\\j\text{ odd}}}
        \binom{k}{j}(2k)^{-j}>1.
      \]
    This shows that $0<c_k<1/2$ for $k\ge3$, since $g_k$ is strictly increasing.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
\label{fact:mixtures}
    Let $k\ge2$, and let $\mathsf P$ be a nonnegative Borel law of finite mean.
    The following statements hold.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
      \item\label{it:mixtures-one} For $0\le\theta\le1$, we have $m(\mathsf P_\theta^+)=(1-\theta)m(\mathsf P)+\theta$ and $1-F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)=(1-\theta)^k[1-F_k(\mathsf P)]$.
      Consequently, $F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)\ge F_k(\mathsf P)$, with equality if and only if $\theta=0$ or $F_k(\mathsf P)=1$.
      \item\label{it:mixtures-zero} For $0\le q\le1$, we have $m(\mathsf P_q^-)=qm(\mathsf P)$ and
      \[
        F_k(\mathsf P_q^-)=\sum_{j=1}^k\binom{k}{j}q^j(1-q)^{k-j}F_j(\mathsf P)
        \ge q^kF_k(\mathsf P).
      \]
      If $0<q<1$, then equality in the inequality holds if and only if $F_j(\mathsf P)=0$ for every $1\le j<k$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The mean formulas follow immediately by linearity.
    For \textup{(i)}, independently replace each of $k$ independent samples from $\mathsf P$ by one with probability $\theta$.
    The resulting sum is less than one exactly when no sample is replaced and the original sum is less than one.
    This proves \textup{(i)}.
    For \textup{(ii)}, retain each sample independently with probability $q$.
    For a fixed set of $j\ge1$ retained indices, independence gives the contribution $q^j(1-q)^{k-j}F_j(\mathsf P)$ to the success probability.
    There are $\binom{k}{j}$ choices of these indices, and the sum is zero when no sample is retained.
    Thus,
    \[
      F_k(\mathsf P_q^-)
      =q^kF_k(\mathsf P)
      +\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k}{j}q^j(1-q)^{k-j}F_j(\mathsf P)
      \ge q^kF_k(\mathsf P).
    \]
    If $0<q<1$, then the coefficient $\binom{k}{j}q^j(1-q)^{k-j}$ of $F_j(\mathsf P)$ is positive for every $1\le j<k$.
    Since $F_j(\mathsf P)\ge0$, the sum over $1\le j<k$ vanishes if and only if $F_j(\mathsf P)=0$ for every $1\le j<k$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:mean-transfer}
  Fix $k\ge2$.
  Suppose that every nonnegative Borel law $\mathsf P$ with $m(\mathsf P)\le\beta_k$ satisfies $F_k(\mathsf P)\le1-(1-\beta_k)^k=(k\beta_k)^k$.
  Then, for every $x\ge0$,
  \[
    \Phi_k(x)=
    \begin{cases}
      \max\{1-(1-x)^k,(kx)^k\}, & 0\le x\le1/k, \\
      1,                        & x\ge1/k.
    \end{cases}
  \]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix any $x\in(0,\beta_k)$, and let $\mathsf P$ be any nonnegative Borel law with $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
  Take $\theta=({\beta_k}-x)/(1-x)$.
  Then $m(\mathsf P_\theta^+)\le\beta_k$.
  By \cref{fact:mixtures}\textup{(i)} and the assumed bound at $\beta_k$,
  \[
    (1-\theta)^k[1-F_k(\mathsf P)]
    =1-F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)\ge(1-\beta_k)^k.
  \]
  Since $1-\theta=(1-\beta_k)/(1-x)$, we obtain $1-F_k(\mathsf P)\ge(1-x)^k$, with equality attained by $\mathsf B_x$.

  Now fix any $x\in(\beta_k,1/k)$, and let $\mathsf P$ be any nonnegative Borel law with $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
  Take $q={\beta_k}/x\in(0,1)$, so $m(\mathsf P_q^-)\le {\beta_k}$.
  Combining \cref{fact:mixtures}\textup{(ii)} with the assumed bound at ${\beta_k}$, we obtain
    \[
      q^kF_k(\mathsf P)\le F_k(\mathsf P_q^-)\le(k{\beta_k})^k.
    \]
  Consequently, $F_k(\mathsf P)\le q^{-k}(k{\beta_k})^k=(kx)^k$, with equality attained by $\mathsf C_{k,x}$.

  The two candidate probabilities $F_k(\mathsf B_x)=1-(1-x)^k$ and $F_k(\mathsf C_{k,x})=(kx)^k$ are equal at $x=\beta_k$.
    For $0<x<\beta_k$, we have $F_k(\mathsf B_x)>F_k(\mathsf C_{k,x})$.
    For $\beta_k<x<1/k$, we have $F_k(\mathsf C_{k,x})>F_k(\mathsf B_x)$.
  The conclusion for $x=\beta_k$ follows from the assumed bound and the two candidate laws.
  At $x=0$, nonnegativity forces $\mathsf P=\delta_0$.
  For $x\ge1/k$, the feasible law $\delta_{1/k}$ attains one.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:portmanteau}
  Let $\mathsf P,\mathsf P_1,\mathsf P_2,\ldots$ be Borel probability measures
  on a metric space $S$. The following conditions are equivalent:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item The laws $\mathsf P_j$ converge weakly to $\mathsf P$.
    \item For every bounded uniformly continuous function
          $f:S\to\mathbb R$, we have $\int_S f\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P_j\longrightarrow\int_S f\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P$.
    \item Each closed set $C\subseteq S$ satisfies $
            \displaystyle\limsup_{j\to\infty}\mathsf P_j(C)\le\mathsf P(C)$.
    \item Each open set $G\subseteq S$ satisfies $\displaystyle\liminf_{j\to\infty}\mathsf P_j(G)\ge\mathsf P(G)$.
    \item For every Borel set $A\subseteq S$ with
          $\mathsf P(\partial_S A)=0$, one has $\mathsf P_j(A)\longrightarrow\mathsf P(A)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- fact-2: body_md -->
\label{fact:weak-convergence}
  The following statements hold for Borel probability laws.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:weak-compactness} For every compact metric space $K$, the space $\mathcal{P}(K)$ is compact and metrizable in the topology of weak convergence.
    In particular, every sequence in $\mathcal{P}(K)$ has a weakly convergent subsequence.
    \item\label{it:weak-products} If $\mathsf P_j,\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ and $\mathsf P_j\Rightarrow\mathsf P$, then $m(\mathsf P_j)\to m(\mathsf P)$ and $\mathsf P_j^{\otimes r}\Rightarrow\mathsf P^{\otimes r}$ for every fixed positive integer $r$.
    \item\label{it:weak-upper-semicontinuity} If $\mathsf P_j,\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ and $\mathsf P_j\Rightarrow\mathsf P$, then $\limsup_{j\to\infty}F_k(\mathsf P_j)\le F_k(\mathsf P)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:attainment}
  For every $x\ge0$, the supremum defining $\Phi_k(x)$ is attained by a law $\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ with $m(\mathsf P)\le x$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By truncation at one, choose laws $\mathsf P_j\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ with $m(\mathsf P_j)\le x$ and $F_k(\mathsf P_j)\to\Phi_k(x)$.
  By \cref{fact:weak-convergence}\textup{(i)}, we may pass to a subsequence such that $\mathsf P_j\Rightarrow\mathsf P$ for some $\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$.
  By \cref{fact:weak-convergence}\textup{(ii)}, we have $m(\mathsf P)=\lim_{j\to\infty}m(\mathsf P_j)\le x$, so $\mathsf P$ is feasible.
  Applying \cref{fact:weak-convergence}\textup{(iii)} gives
  \[
    \Phi_k(x)
    =\lim_{j\to\infty}F_k(\mathsf P_j)
    \le F_k(\mathsf P)
    \le\Phi_k(x).
  \]
  Thus, $\mathsf P$ attains $\Phi_k(x)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:kellerer-duality}
  Let $\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$, and let $h:[0,1]^k\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and upper semicontinuous.
  Then
  \[
    \sup_{\mathsf G\in\Pi_k(\mathsf P)}\int h\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf G
    =
    \inf\left\{
    \sum_{i=1}^k\int\varphi_i\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P:
    \begin{array}{l}
      \varphi_i:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\text{ are upper semicontinuous}, \\
      \varphi_i\text{ are integrable},                             \\
      \sum_{i=1}^k\varphi_i(z_i)\ge h(z)\text{ for every }z\in[0,1]^k
    \end{array}
    \right\}.
  \]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:duality}
  For every $\mathsf P\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$,
  \[
    T_k(\mathsf P)
    =\inf\left\{k\int w\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P:
    \begin{array}{l}
      w:[0,1]\to[0,1]\text{ is Borel measurable}, \\
      \sum_{i=1}^k w(z_i)\ge1\text{ for every }z\in H_k
    \end{array}\right\}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Applying \cref{thm:kellerer-duality} with $h=\1_{H_k}$, we obtain
  \[
    T_k(\mathsf P)
    =
    \inf\left\{
    \sum_{i=1}^k\int\varphi_i\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P:
    \sum_{i=1}^k\varphi_i(z_i)\ge \1_{H_k}(z)
    \text{ for every }z\in[0,1]^k
    \right\}.
  \]
  Here the infimum is over upper semicontinuous, $\mathsf P$-integrable functions $\varphi_i:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$, $1\le i\le k$.
  For any admissible family $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k$, set $w=k^{-1}\sum_i\varphi_i$.
  Averaging $\sum_i\varphi_i(z_i)\ge\1_{H_k}(z)$ over all coordinate permutations, we obtain $\sum_iw(z_i)\ge\1_{H_k}(z)$ for every $z\in[0,1]^k$.
  Taking $z=(t,\ldots,t)$ shows $kw(t)\ge0$, so $w\ge0$.
  Replacing $w$ by $w\wedge1$ preserves the covering condition and does not increase its integral.
  \[
    \inf_{\text{covers}} k\int w\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P
    \le
    \inf_{\text{dual feasible }(\varphi_i)}
    \sum_{i=1}^k \int \varphi_i\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P
    =
    T_k(\mathsf P).
  \]

  Conversely, let $w:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be any Borel measurable function satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^k w(z_i)\ge1$ for every $z\in H_k$.
  For every $\mathsf G\in\Pi_k(\mathsf P)$, we have
  \[
    \mathsf G(H_k)
    \le\int\sum_{i=1}^k w(z_i)\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf G(z)
    =k\int w\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P.
  \]
  Taking the maximum over $\mathsf G\in\Pi_k(\mathsf P)$ and then the infimum over all such $w$ gives $T_k(\mathsf P)\le\inf_w k\int w\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P$, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:normalization}
  Fix $k\ge2$ and $0<x<1/k$.
  Let $\mathsf P$ be a nonnegative Borel law maximizing $F_k$ under $m(\mathsf P)\le x$, and set $a=kx$.
  Then the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:normalization-support} The law $\mathsf P$ is supported on $[0,1]$ and has mean $x$.
    \item\label{it:normalization-mixture} There is a law $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ of mean $1/k$ such that $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$.
    In particular, $\mathsf P(\{0\})\ge1-a$.
    \item\label{it:normalization-coupling} The law $\mathsf Q$ admits an exchangeable coupling whose sum is one almost surely.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
First suppose that $\mathsf P$ is supported on $[0,1]$.
  {If $m(\mathsf P)<x$, then take $\theta=(x-m(\mathsf P))/(1-m(\mathsf P))\in(0,1)$.
  Then $m(\mathsf P_\theta^+)=x$.
  Since $F_k(\mathsf P)\le kx<1$ and $0<\theta<1$, it follows from $1-F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)=(1-\theta)^k[1-F_k(\mathsf P)]$ that $F_k(\mathsf P_\theta^+)>F_k(\mathsf P)$, a contradiction.
  Thus, $m(\mathsf P)=x$.}

  Suppose that $T_k(\mathsf P)<kx$.
  By \cref{lem:duality}, there exists a Borel measurable map $w:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ such that $\int w\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P<x$ and
  \[
    \sum_{i=1}^k w(z_i)\ge1
    \text{ for every }(z_1,\ldots,z_k)\in[0,1]^k
    \text{ with }\sum_{i=1}^k z_i\ge1.
  \]
  For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with law $\mathsf P$, the variables $w(X_i)$ are independent with the common law $\mathsf{L}(w(X_1))$, whose mean is less than $x$.
  The covering condition implies that $\sum_iX_i\ge1$ forces $\sum_iw(X_i)\ge1$, so this new law has success probability at least $F_k(\mathsf P)$.
  This new law is therefore also maximizing, but its mean is strictly less than $x$, a contradiction.
  Therefore, $T_k(\mathsf P)=kx$.

  Average an optimal coupling over all coordinate permutations, and denote the resulting coordinates by $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_k$.
  The averaged coupling is exchangeable and still has marginal law $\mathsf P$ in every coordinate.
  Coordinate permutations preserve the sum, so the averaged coupling remains optimal.
  Writing $\widetilde S=\sum_{i=1}^k\widetilde X_i$, we have $\mathbb{E}\widetilde S=kx=T_k(\mathsf P)=\mathbb{P}(\widetilde S\ge1)$, while
  \[
    \mathbb{E}\widetilde S-\mathbb{P}(\widetilde S\ge1)
    =\mathbb{E}[\widetilde S\1_{\{\widetilde S<1\}}]
    +\mathbb{E}[(\widetilde S-1)\1_{\{\widetilde S\ge1\}}].
  \]
  Both terms on the right are nonnegative and therefore vanish.
  Thus, $\widetilde S\in\{0,1\}$ almost surely.
  On $\{\widetilde S=0\}$ every coordinate is zero.
  The event $\{\widetilde S=1\}$ has probability $kx=a$, and exchangeability makes its conditional marginals equal to a law $\mathsf Q$ of mean $1/k$.
  Decomposing a marginal over $\{\widetilde S=0\}$ and $\{\widetilde S=1\}$, we obtain $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$.
  The conditional joint law on $\{\widetilde S=1\}$ is the required constant-sum coupling.
  The mixture formula also gives $\mathsf P(\{0\})=1-a+a\mathsf Q(\{0\})\ge1-a$.

  For a general maximizing law, let $X$ have law $\mathsf P$.
  Truncation at one preserves success, so the law of $X\wedge1$ is maximizing and, by the bounded case, has mean $x$.
  Since $x=\mathbb{E}(X\wedge1)\le\mathbb{E} X\le x$, we have $\mathbb{E}(X-1)_+=0$.
  Thus, $\mathsf P$ is supported on $[0,1]$, and all the conclusions follow from the bounded case.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:safe-cap}
  Let $X_1,\ldots,X_j$ be independent nonnegative variables with finite support, sum $S$, and $p=\mathbb{P}(S<1)>0$.
  Suppose that $\max_{1\le i\le j}|\operatorname{supp} X_i|\ge2$.
  Then there exist $i\in\{1,\ldots,j\}$ and $\tau\in\operatorname{supp} X_i$ with $\tau<\max\operatorname{supp} X_i$ such that the following statements hold after replacing $X_i$ by $X_i'=X_i\wedge\tau$ and leaving all other coordinates unchanged.
  Write $S'=\sum_hX_h'$, $p'=\mathbb{P}(S'<1)$, $r'=1-\mathbb{E}[S'\mid S'<1]$, $B'=\mathbb{E} S'-\mathbb{E}[S'\mid S'<1]$, and $\zeta=B-B'$.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:safe-cap-deficit} We have $r'\ge r$, $|\operatorname{supp} X_i'|<|\operatorname{supp} X_i|$, and $\sum_{h=1}^j|\operatorname{supp} X_h'|<\sum_{h=1}^j|\operatorname{supp} X_h|$.
    \item\label{it:safe-cap-loss} We have $p'\ge p>0$ and
    \[
      r'-r=\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+-\zeta,\text{ }
      p'(r-\zeta)\le pr
      \text{ and }0\le\zeta\le\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
First consider any index $i$ and cap $\tau\ge0$, using the primed notation in the statement.
  Then $S'=S-X_i+(X_i\wedge\tau)$.
  Since $S'\le S$, we have $p'\ge p>0$, so these parameters, namely $r'$, $B'$, and $\zeta$, are defined.
  The loss of mean is
  $\mathbb{E} S-\mathbb{E} S'=\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+$.
  For each sample, the increase in $(1-S)_+$ is zero unless
  $X_i>\tau$ and $S-X_i+\tau<1$.
  When both conditions hold, the increase is at most $X_i-\tau$.
  By independence of $X_i$ and $S-X_i$, we therefore have
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      p'r'-pr
       & =\mathbb{E}[(1-S')_+-(1-S)_+]                    \\
       & \le\mathbb{E}[(X_i-\tau)_+\1_{\{S-X_i+\tau<1\}}] \\
       & =\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+\mathbb{P}(S-X_i+\tau<1)       \\
       & \le p'\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The last inequality follows from
  $\{S-X_i+\tau<1\}\subseteq\{S'<1\}$, since $X_i\wedge \tau\le \tau$.
  Using $r=1-\mathbb{E} S+B$ and $r'=1-\mathbb{E} S'+B'$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:cap-basic}
    r'-r=\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+-\zeta
    \text{ and }
    p'(r-\zeta)\le pr.
  \end{equation}
  Since $p'\ge p>0$, the second inequality implies
  $\zeta\ge r(1-p/p')\ge0$.
  If $r'\ge r$, then the first identity also implies
  $\zeta\le\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+$.
  Thus a truncation that does not decrease $r$ satisfies
  $0\le\zeta\le\mathbb{E}(X_i-\tau)_+$.


  Recall that, for a finitely supported random variable $X$, $\operatorname{supp} X=\{t:\mathbb{P}(X=t)>0\}$ and $|\operatorname{supp} X|$ is the number of points in this set.
  In particular, $|\operatorname{supp} X|=1$ means that $X$ is almost surely constant.
  Since
  $\sum_{h=1}^j\operatorname{Cov}(S,X_h\mid S<1)=\operatorname{Var}(S\mid S<1)\ge0$
  and $\operatorname{Cov}(S,X_h\mid S<1)=0$ whenever $|\operatorname{supp} X_h|=1$,
  there is an index $i\in\{1,\ldots,j\}$ such that
  $|\operatorname{supp} X_i|\ge2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(S,X_i\mid S<1)\ge0$.
  Fix one such index $i$.

  Write $T=S-X_i$ and $\operatorname{supp} X_i=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}$,
  where $0\le x_1<\cdots<x_N$ and $N\ge2$.
  For $t\ge0$, define
  $K(t)=\mathbb{E}[(1-r-T-t)\1_{\{T+t<1\}}]$,
  where the expectation is over $T$.
  By independence of $T$ and $X_i$ and the equality $r=1-\mathbb{E}[S\mid S<1]$, we have
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \mathbb{E} K(X_i)
       & =
      \mathbb{E}\left[
        \mathbb{E}_T\left[
          (1-r-T-X_i)\1_{\{T+X_i<1\}}
          \,\middle|\, X_i
          \right]
      \right]                        \\
       & =
      \mathbb{E}\left[
        (1-r-T-X_i)\1_{\{T+X_i<1\}}
      \right]                        \\
       & =
      \mathbb{E}\left[
        (1-r-S)\1_{\{S<1\}}
      \right]                        \\
       & =
      \mathbb{P}(S<1)
      \left(1-r-\mathbb{E}[S\mid S<1]\right) \\
       & =0.
    \end{aligned}
  \]


  Set $A_0=0$ and
  $A_q=\mathbb{E}[K(X_i)\1_{\{X_i\le x_q\}}]$ for $1\le q\le N$.
  Then $A_N=\mathbb{E} K(X_i)=0$.
  By summation by parts and the choice of $i$, we have
  \[
    \sum_{q=1}^{N-1}(x_{q+1}-x_q)A_q
    =-\mathbb{E}[X_iK(X_i)]
    =p\operatorname{Cov}(S,X_i\mid S<1)\ge0.
  \]
  Every coefficient $x_{q+1}-x_q$ is positive.
  Hence there is a $q\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}$ such that $A_q\ge0$.
  Choose the least such $q$.
  Then $A_{q-1}\le0$, and
  $K(x_q)=(A_q-A_{q-1})/\mathbb{P}(X_i=x_q)\ge0$.

  Set $\tau=x_q$, so that $\tau\in\operatorname{supp} X_i$ and
  $\tau<\max\operatorname{supp} X_i$.
  Define $X_i'=X_i\wedge\tau$ and $X_h'=X_h$ for $h\ne i$.
  The variable $X_i'$ remains independent of $T$.
  Since $S'=\sum_{h=1}^jX_h'=T+X_i'$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      p'(r'-r)
       & =p'r'-p'r                                 \\
       & =\mathbb{E}[(1-S')\1_{\{S'<1\}}]
      -\mathbb{E}[r\1_{\{S'<1\}}]                          \\
       & =\mathbb{E}[(1-r-S')\1_{\{S'<1\}}]                \\
       & =\mathbb{E}[(1-r-T-X_i')\1_{\{T+X_i'<1\}}]        \\
       & =\mathbb{E} K(X_i')                               \\
       & =\mathbb{E}\left[K(X_i)\1_{\{X_i\le x_q\}}\right]
      +K(x_q)\mathbb{P}(X_i>x_q)                        \\
       & =A_q+\mathbb{P}(X_i>x_q)K(x_q)                 \\
       & \ge0,
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Thus $r'\ge r$, since $p'\ge p>0$.
  The truncation leaves each value $x_1,\ldots,x_q$ unchanged
  and replaces every value $x_{q+1},\ldots,x_N$ by $x_q$.
  Therefore $\operatorname{supp} X_i'=\{x_1,\ldots,x_q\}$, so
  $|\operatorname{supp} X_i'|=q<N=|\operatorname{supp} X_i|$.
  For every $h\ne i$, we have $\operatorname{supp} X_h'=\operatorname{supp} X_h$.
  Consequently,
  $\sum_{h=1}^j|\operatorname{supp} X_h'|<\sum_{h=1}^j|\operatorname{supp} X_h|$.
  Together with \eqref{eq:cap-basic}, $p'\ge p>0$ and $r'\ge r$ give \textup{(ii)}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:product}
  Let $j\ge1$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_j$ be independent bounded nonnegative variables with sum $S$.
  Suppose that $p=\mathbb{P}(S<1)>0$, and write $r=1-\mathbb{E}[S\mid S<1]$.
  If $r>\max_{1\le i\le j}\mathbb{E} X_i$, then there are $z_i\in[0,\mathbb{E} X_i]$, $1\le i\le j$, such that
  $\sum_{i=1}^jz_i=\mathbb{E} S-\mathbb{E}[S\mid S<1]$ and
  $
    p\ge\prod_{i=1}^j\left(1-\frac{z_i}{r}\right).
  $
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
First suppose that every coordinate has finite support.
  If $|\operatorname{supp} X_i|=1$ for every $i$, then $S$ is constant.
  Since $p>0$, we have $p=1$ and $B=0$, so the conclusion holds
  with $z_i=0$ for every $i$.

  Otherwise, set $X_i^{(0)}=X_i$.
  For the variables after $n$ truncations, define
  $S^{(n)}=\sum_{i=1}^jX_i^{(n)}$,
  $p^{(n)}=\mathbb{P}(S^{(n)}<1)$,
  $r^{(n)}=1-\mathbb{E}[S^{(n)}\mid S^{(n)}<1]$,
  $B^{(n)}=\mathbb{E} S^{(n)}-\mathbb{E}[S^{(n)}\mid S^{(n)}<1]$, and
  $L_n=\sum_{i=1}^j|\operatorname{supp} X_i^{(n)}|$.
  Initially, $S^{(0)}=S$, $p^{(0)}=p$, $r^{(0)}=r$,
  $B^{(0)}=B$, and $L_0>j$.

  Whenever $L_n>j$, some coordinate has at least two support points.
  By \cref{lem:safe-cap}, we can choose an index $i_n$ and a point
  $\tau_n\in\operatorname{supp} X_{i_n}^{(n)}$ with
  $\tau_n<\max\operatorname{supp} X_{i_n}^{(n)}$ such that, setting
  $X_{i_n}^{(n+1)}=X_{i_n}^{(n)}\wedge\tau_n$ and
  $X_h^{(n+1)}=X_h^{(n)}$ for $h\ne i_n$, we have
  $r^{(n+1)}\ge r^{(n)}$ and $L_{n+1}\le L_n-1$.
  Each truncation preserves independence, nonnegativity, and finite
  support. Since $S^{(n+1)}\le S^{(n)}$, we also have
  $p^{(n+1)}\ge p^{(n)}\ge p>0$.
  Thus, the conditional parameters remain defined, and the current variables satisfy the hypotheses of \cref{lem:safe-cap} whenever $L_n>j$.
  Moreover, $r^{(n)}\ge r>0$ throughout the procedure.

  Since $L_n\ge j$, the procedure stops after some
  $N\le L_0-j$ steps with $L_N=j$.
  At each step, the index $i_n$ and threshold $\tau_n$ are chosen from the current distributions, not from the sampled values.
    Once these choices and the initial distributions are fixed, $N$ is a fixed integer and does not depend on the sample.
  Each support is nonempty, so $|\operatorname{supp} X_i^{(N)}|=1$ for every $i$.
  Hence $S^{(N)}$ is constant.
  Since $p^{(N)}>0$, this constant is less than one, so
  $p^{(N)}=1$ and
  $\mathbb{E}[S^{(N)}\mid S^{(N)}<1]=\mathbb{E} S^{(N)}$.
  Therefore $B^{(N)}=0$.

  For $0\le n<N$, set $\zeta_n=B^{(n)}-B^{(n+1)}$.
  Since $p^{(n+1)}\ge p^{(n)}>0$ and $r^{(n+1)}\ge r^{(n)}$, \cref{lem:safe-cap} gives
  \[
    0\le r^{(n)}\left(1-\frac{p^{(n)}}{p^{(n+1)}}\right)
    \le\zeta_n
    \le\mathbb{E} X_{i_n}^{(n)}-\mathbb{E} X_{i_n}^{(n+1)}.
  \]
  Moreover, since $r^{(n)}\ge r>0$ and $\zeta_n\ge0$, \cref{lem:safe-cap} yields
  \[
    p^{(n)}
    \ge p^{(n+1)}\left(1-\frac{\zeta_n}{r^{(n)}}\right)
    \ge p^{(n+1)}\left(1-\frac{\zeta_n}{r}\right).
  \]

  For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,j\}$, set
  $z_i=\sum_{0\le n<N:\,i_n=i}\zeta_n$.
  Since $X_i^{(n+1)}=X_i^{(n)}$ whenever $i_n\ne i$, summing the mean losses at the steps with $i_n=i$ gives
  \[
    0\le z_i\le\mathbb{E} X_i-\mathbb{E} X_i^{(N)}\le\mathbb{E} X_i.
  \]
  Each $\zeta_n$ occurs in exactly one $z_i$, so
  \[
    \sum_{i=1}^jz_i=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\zeta_n=B^{(0)}-B^{(N)}=B.
  \]

  For each $i$, we have
  $\sum_{0\le n<N:\,i_n=i}\zeta_n/r=z_i/r\le\mathbb{E} X_i/r<1$.
  Since every $\zeta_n$ is nonnegative, all factors
  $1-\zeta_n/r$ are positive.
  Iterating $p^{(n)}\ge p^{(n+1)}(1-\zeta_n/r)$ for $0\le n<N$, using $p^{(N)}=1$, and grouping the factors by coordinate, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      p=p^{(0)}
       & \ge p^{(N)}
      \prod_{n=0}^{N-1}\left(1-\frac{\zeta_n}{r}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^j
      \prod_{\substack{0\le n<N        \\i_n=i}}
      \left(1-\frac{\zeta_n}{r}\right) \\
       & \ge\prod_{i=1}^j
      \left(1-\sum_{\substack{0\le n<N \\i_n=i}}
      \frac{\zeta_n}{r}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^j\left(1-\frac{z_i}{r}\right).
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The last inequality applies
  $\prod_h(1-u_h)\ge1-\sum_hu_h$
  to each coordinate separately, with $u_h\ge0$ and
  $\sum_hu_h<1$.
  For a coordinate that is never truncated, the corresponding
  sum is zero and the product is one.
  This proves the finite-support case.

  Now consider arbitrary bounded nonnegative coordinates.
  For each integer $h\ge1$, set $X_i^{(h)}=2^{-h}\lceil2^{h}X_i\rceil$ and
  $S_{h}=\sum_{i=1}^jX_i^{(h)}$.
  Here $h$ is a new approximation index, distinct from the fixed number of truncations $N$ above.
  These rounded variables remain independent and have finite support.
  Moreover, $X_i^{(h)}\downarrow X_i$ and
  $0\le X_i^{(h)}-X_i<2^{-h}$.
  It follows that $\{S_{h}<1\}\uparrow\{S<1\}$ and
  $(1-S_{h})_+\uparrow(1-S)_+$.
  In particular, a sample with $S=1$ belongs to none of the rounded
  failure events.

  Write $p_{h}=\mathbb{P}(S_{h}<1)$.
  By monotone convergence, we have $p_{h}\uparrow p$ and
  $\mathbb{E}(1-S_{h})_+\to pr$.
  For all sufficiently large $h$, we therefore have $p_{h}>0$ and
  $r_{h}=\mathbb{E}(1-S_{h})_+/p_{h}\to r$.
  The bound on the rounding error also implies
  $\mathbb{E} X_i^{(h)}\to\mathbb{E} X_i$ for each $i$.
  Since $r>\max_i\mathbb{E} X_i$, we have
  $r_{h}>\max_i\mathbb{E} X_i^{(h)}$ for all sufficiently large $h$.

For each sufficiently large $h$, there exist numbers
$z_i^{(h)}\in[0,\mathbb{E} X_i^{(h)}]$, $1\le i\le j$, such that
$\sum_{i=1}^j z_i^{(h)}=\mathbb{E} S_h-1+r_h$ and
$p_h\ge\prod_{i=1}^j\left(1-z_i^{(h)}/r_h\right)$.
  These vectors are uniformly bounded, so a subsequence converges
  to a vector $(z_i)_{i=1}^j$.
  Passing to the limit along this subsequence in $0\le z_i^{(h)}\le\mathbb{E} X_i^{(h)}$ and $\sum_i z_i^{(h)}=\mathbb{E} S_{h}-1+r_{h}$, we obtain $0\le z_i\le\mathbb{E} X_i$ and $\sum_i z_i=\mathbb{E} S-1+r=B$.
  Since $p_{h}\to p$ and $r_{h}\to r>0$, we also obtain $p\ge\prod_i(1-z_i/r)$.
  This proves the result for the original variables.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:gamma}
  Under the hypotheses and notation of \cref{lem:product}, suppose that $\mathbb{E} X_i=m>0$ for $1\le i\le j$ and $jm\le1$.
  For $\ell\in\{0,\ldots,j-1\}$, if $1-(j-\ell)m\le r\le1-(j-\ell-1)m$, then
  \[
    p\ge\left(1-\frac{m}{r}\right)^\ell
    \frac{1-(j-\ell)m}{r}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:product}, choose numbers $z_i\in[0,m]$, $1\le i\le j$, satisfying $\sum_i z_i=B=r-1+jm$ and $p\ge\prod_i(1-z_i/r)$.
  If two coordinates satisfy $0<u\le v<m$, then set $\varepsilon=\min\{u,m-v\}>0$ and replace them by $u-\varepsilon,v+\varepsilon$.
  Their sum is unchanged, and
  \[
    \left(1-\frac{u-\varepsilon}{r}\right)
    \left(1-\frac{v+\varepsilon}{r}\right)
    =\left(1-\frac ur\right)\left(1-\frac vr\right)
    -\frac{\varepsilon(v-u+\varepsilon)}{r^2}.
  \]
  Since $r>m$, all other factors are positive, so the product does not increase.
  Each step moves at least one coordinate in $(0,m)$ to $0$ or $m$.
  After finitely many steps, at most one coordinate lies in $(0,m)$.
  The hypothesis on $r$ is equivalent to $\ell m\le B\le(\ell+1)m$.
  Thus the resulting coordinates, up to permutation, are $\ell$ copies of $m$, one copy of $B-\ell m$, and zeros.
  Consequently,
  \[
    p\ge\left(1-\frac mr\right)^\ell
    \left(1-\frac{B-\ell m}{r}\right)
    =\left(1-\frac mr\right)^\ell\frac{1-(j-\ell)m}{r}.
  \]
  The same result holds at either interval endpoint, where the remaining coordinate is $0$ or $m$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- fact-3: body_md -->
\label{fact:retained-sums}
  Let $k\ge2$ and $0<x<1/k$, and let $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ have mean $1/k$.
  Set $a=kx$ and $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$, and use the notation $R_j,f_j,e_j,w,b_j$ above.
  For independent $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ with law $\mathsf P$, set $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kX_i$.
  Then the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:retained-sums-mixture} We have
    \[
      \begin{aligned}
        F_k(\mathsf P)     & =a^k\left(f_k+\sum_{j<k}b_jf_j\right),         \\
        F_{k-1}(\mathsf P) & =a^{k-1}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{j}
        \left(\frac{1-a}{a}\right)^{k-1-j}f_j,                              \\
        \mathbb{E}(S_k-1)_+        & =\frac{a^k}{k}\left(w+\sum_{j<k}b_je_j\right).
      \end{aligned}
    \]
    \item\label{it:retained-sums-budget} We have $e_1=0$ and $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$ for $1\le j<k$.
    In particular, $\sum_{j<k}f_j\le w$.
    \item\label{it:retained-sums-maximality} If $\mathsf P$ is maximizing under the mean bound $x$, then $\sum_{j<k}b_jf_j\ge1-f_k$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
For $1\le j\le k$, the probability that exactly $j$ samples are retained is $\binom{k}{j}a^j(1-a)^{k-j}$.
  Conditional on exactly $j$ samples being retained, $S_k$ has the same distribution as $R_j$, because the $Y_i$'s are i.i.d. and independent of the $I_i$'s.
  When no samples are retained, $S_k=0$, so summing over $1\le j\le k$ gives
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:thinning}
    \begin{aligned}
      F_k(\mathsf P)
       & =\sum_{j=1}^k\binom{k}{j}a^j(1-a)^{k-j}f_j
      =a^k\left(f_k+\sum_{j<k}b_jf_j\right),            \\
      \mathbb{E}(S_k-1)_+
       & =\frac{a^k}{k}\left(w+\sum_{j<k}b_je_j\right).
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  The same conditioning with $k-1$ samples gives the stated formula for $F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)$.

  Since $Y_1\le1$, we have $e_1=0$.
  For $1\le j<k$, the increment $(R_{j+1}-1)_+-(R_j-1)_+$ equals $Y_{j+1}$ on $\{R_j\ge1\}$ and is nonnegative otherwise.
  Independence and $\mathbb{E} Y_{j+1}=1/k$ therefore give $e_{j+1}-e_j\ge k\mathbb{E}[Y_{j+1}\1_{\{R_j\ge1\}}]=f_j$.
  Consequently,
  \[
    e_1=0\text{ and }e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j
  \]
  for $1\le j\le k-1$.
  In particular, summing yields $\sum_{j<k}f_j\le w$.


  If $\mathsf P$ is maximizing, then $F_k(\mathsf P)\ge F_k(\mathsf C_{k,x})=a^k$, so \eqref{eq:thinning} implies $\sum_{j<k}b_jf_j\ge1-f_k$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- fact-4: body_md -->
\label{fact:comparison-arrays}
  Let $k\ge2$, and use the comparison values $e_j^{(s)},f_j^{(s)}$ and their interpolants $e_j^*,f_j^*$ defined above.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:comparison-node-arrays} For $1\le s\le k$ and $1\le j\le k$,
    \[
      (e_j^{(s)},f_j^{(s)})=
      \begin{cases}
        (0,0),                                                & j\le k-s, \\
        \bigl(j-k+s(1-1/s)^{j-k+s},\,1-(1-1/s)^{j-k+s}\bigr), & j>k-s.
      \end{cases}
    \]
    Moreover, $e_1^{(s)}=0$, $e_{j+1}^{(s)}=e_j^{(s)}+f_j^{(s)}$ for $1\le j<k$, and $e_k^{(s)}=\sum_{j<k}f_j^{(s)}=W_s$.
    \item\label{it:comparison-interpolated-budget} For $0\le w\le W_k$, we have
    \[
      \begin{aligned}
        e_1^*(w) & =0,\text{ }e_{j+1}^*(w)=e_j^*(w)+f_j^*(w)\quad(1\le j<k), \\
        e_k^*(w) & =w=\sum_{j<k}f_j^*(w).
      \end{aligned}
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
For $j\le k-s$, we have $R_j^{(s)}=j/k\le(k-s)/k<1$.
  For $j>k-s$, set $N=\sum_{i=k-s+1}^jJ_i$.
  Then $N$ is binomial with parameters $j-k+s$ and $1/s$, and $R_j^{(s)}=(k-s)/k+(s/k)N$.
  Since $R_j^{(s)}-1=(s/k)(N-1)$, we have $f_j^{(s)}=\mathbb{P}(N\ge1)=1-\mathbb{P}(N=0)$.
  Since $N$ is a nonnegative integer, $(N-1)_+=N-1+\1_{\{N=0\}}$, so $e_j^{(s)}=s\mathbb{E}(N-1)_+=s(\mathbb{E} N-1+\mathbb{P}(N=0))$.
  Substituting $\mathbb{E} N=(j-k+s)/s$ and $\mathbb{P}(N=0)=(1-1/s)^{j-k+s}$ gives the formula in \textup{(i)}.
  Taking differences $e_{j+1}^{(s)}-e_j^{(s)}$ for $1\le j<k$ and evaluating $e_j^{(s)}$ at $j=k$, we obtain
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:alignment}
    e_{j+1}^{(s)}=e_j^{(s)}+f_j^{(s)}
    \text{ for $1\le j\le k-1$ and }e_k^{(s)}=W_s.
  \end{equation}
  Summing \eqref{eq:alignment} and using $e_1^{(s)}=0$, we obtain $\sum_{j<k}f_j^{(s)}=W_s$ for every integer $s$ with $1\le s\le k$.
  \textup{(ii)} follows by taking the same affine combinations of the relations in \textup{(i)}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:product-shortfall}
  Let $k\ge2$.
  The following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:product-shortfall-pointwise} For $y_1,\ldots,y_k\in[0,1]$, we have
    \[
      \left(1-\sum_{i=1}^ky_i\right)_+\le\prod_{i=1}^k(1-y_i).
    \]
    The inequality is strict if $0<y_i<1$ for every $1\le i\le k$.
    \item\label{it:product-shortfall-expectation} Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_j$ be independent $[0,1]$-valued variables of mean $1/k$, where $1\le j\le k$.
    Set $R_j=\sum_{i=1}^jY_i$ and $e_j=k\mathbb{E}(R_j-1)_+$.
    Then
    \[
      \begin{aligned}
        \mathbb{E}(1-R_j)_+ & =\frac{k-j+e_j}{k}\le\left(1-\frac1k\right)^j, \\
        0\le e_j    & \le k\left(1-\frac1k\right)^j-(k-j).
      \end{aligned}
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
If $\sum_{i=1}^k y_i\ge1$, then the left-hand side is zero and the right-hand side is nonnegative, so the inequality holds.
  If $\sum_{i=1}^k y_i<1$, then induction using $(1-u)(1-v)=1-u-v+uv\ge1-u-v$ proves the inequality.

  Now suppose that $0<y_i<1$ for every $1\le i\le k$.
  If $\sum_{i=1}^k y_i\ge1$, then $(1-\sum_{i=1}^k y_i)_+=0<\prod_{i=1}^k(1-y_i)$.
  If $\sum_{i=1}^k y_i<1$, then applying the non-strict inequality to $0,y_2,\ldots,y_k$ gives
  \[
    \prod_{i=1}^k(1-y_i)
    \ge(1-y_1)\left(1-\sum_{i=2}^k y_i\right)
    >1-\sum_{i=1}^k y_i,
  \]
  since $y_1\sum_{i=2}^k y_i>0$.

  For \textup{(ii)}, by \textup{(i)} applied with $y_i=Y_i$ for $1\le i\le j$ and $y_i=0$ for $j<i\le k$, we have $(1-R_j)_+\le\prod_{i=1}^j(1-Y_i)$ almost surely.
  Taking expectations and using the independence of $Y_1,\ldots,Y_j$ and their common mean $1/k$, we obtain
  \[
    \frac{k-j+e_j}{k}
    =\mathbb{E}(1-R_j)_+
    \le\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^j(1-Y_i)
    =\prod_{i=1}^j\mathbb{E}(1-Y_i)
    =\left(1-\frac1k\right)^j.
  \]
  The bound on $e_j$ follows by rearranging.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- fact-5: body_md -->
\label{fact:retained-shortfall}
  Let $k\ge2$ and $1\le j\le k$.
  Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_j$ be independent $[0,1]$-valued variables of mean $1/k$.
  Set $R_j=\sum_{i=1}^jY_i$, $f_j=\mathbb{P}(R_j\ge1)$, and $e_j=k\mathbb{E}(R_j-1)_+$.
  Suppose that $f_j<1$, and write $r_j=\mathbb{E}[1-R_j\mid R_j<1]$.
  Then the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{it:retained-shortfall-mean} We have $k(1-f_j)r_j=k-j+e_j$.
    \item\label{it:retained-shortfall-inversion} If $2\le j\le k$ and $\ell=k-j$, then $\ell+e_j$ belongs to the domain of $\Psi_\ell^{-1}$ and
    \[
      kr_j\le\Psi_\ell^{-1}(\ell+e_j)
      \text{ and }
      1-f_j\ge\frac{\ell+e_j}{\Psi_\ell^{-1}(\ell+e_j)}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Since $\mathbb{E} R_j=j/k$ and $(1-z)_+=1-z+(z-1)_+$, we have $\mathbb{E}(1-R_j)_+=(k-j+e_j)/k$.
  By the definitions of $f_j$ and $r_j$, we have $(1-f_j)r_j=\mathbb{E}(1-R_j)_+$, and hence
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:retained-shortfall-identity}
    k(1-f_j)r_j=k-j+e_j.
  \end{equation}


  Fix $2\le j\le k$ with $f_j<1$, and set $\ell=k-j$.
  To prove \textup{(ii)}, it suffices by \eqref{eq:retained-shortfall-identity} to show that $kr_j\le\Psi_\ell^{-1}(\ell+e_j)$.
  By \cref{lem:product-shortfall}\textup{(ii)}, $\ell+e_j$ lies in the domain of $\Psi_\ell^{-1}$, and $\Psi_\ell^{-1}(\ell+e_j)\ge \ell+1$.
  If $kr_j\le \ell+1$, then $kr_j\le\Psi_\ell^{-1}(\ell+e_j)$, proving the desired result.

  Suppose that $kr_j>\ell+1$.
  Since $r_j\le1$, choose an integer $\sigma$ with $\ell+1\le\sigma<k$ such that $\sigma\le kr_j\le\sigma+1$.
  Applying \cref{lem:gamma} to $Y_1,\ldots,Y_j$ with $m=1/k$ and index $\sigma-\ell\in\{1,\ldots,j-1\}$, and using \eqref{eq:retained-shortfall-identity}, we obtain
  \[
    \ell+e_j=k(1-f_j)r_j
    \ge\sigma\left(1-\frac1{kr_j}\right)^{\sigma-\ell}
    =\Psi_\ell(kr_j).
  \]
  Since $\Psi_\ell^{-1}$ is increasing, we again have $kr_j\le\Psi_\ell^{-1}(\ell+e_j)$.
  Thus, \textup{(ii)} follows from \eqref{eq:retained-shortfall-identity}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:capacities}
          For every $1\le j<k$, the function $C_j$ is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and concave, and satisfies $f_j\le C_j(e_j)$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The function $C_1$ is constant, and $f_1=\mathbb{P}(Y_1=1)\le\mathbb{E} Y_1=1/k=C_1(e_1)$.
          Thus, it suffices to prove the desired result for $j\ge2$.
          Fix $2\le j<k$ from now on.

          We first show that $C_j$ is nondecreasing and concave.
          To compare the slopes of the segments defining $C_j$, we regard $e_j^{(s)}$ and $f_j^{(s)}$ as functions of a real variable $s\ge \ell+1$ using \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(i)}.
          Let
          \[
            g(s)=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\log(1-f_j^{(s)})
            =\log\frac{s}{s-1}-\frac{s-\ell}{s(s-1)}.
          \]
          Since $\ell=k-j\ge1$ and $s\ge\ell+1\ge2$, the power series for $-\log(1-1/s)$ and direct differentiation give
          \[
            g(s)=\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac{\ell-1+1/m}{s^m}
            \text{ and }
            g'(s)=\frac{\ell-(2\ell-1)s}{s^2(s-1)^2}.
          \]
          The lower bound for $g(s)$ follows from the first term, while comparison with $\ell\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}s^{-m}=\ell/(s(s-1))$ proves the strict upper bound because $0<\ell-1+1/m<\ell$ for $m\ge2$.
          Substituting $g(s)<\ell/(s(s-1))$ into $g'(s)+g(s)^2$ and using $s\ge\ell+1$, we obtain
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              \frac{\ell-1/2}{s^2}
               & \le g(s)<\frac{\ell}{s(s-1)}\le\frac1s,    \\
              g'(s)+g(s)^2
               & <\frac{\ell^2+\ell-(2\ell-1)s}{s^2(s-1)^2}
              \le\frac{1-\ell^2}{s^2(s-1)^2}\le0.
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          Consequently,
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}e_j^{(s)} & =(1-f_j^{(s)})(1-sg(s))>0,           \\
              \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}f_j^{(s)} & =(1-f_j^{(s)})g(s)>0,                \\
              \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d} f_j^{(s)}/\mathrm{d} s}{\mathrm{d} e_j^{(s)}/\mathrm{d} s}\right)
                                         & =\frac{g'(s)+g(s)^2}{(1-sg(s))^2}<0.
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          By the Cauchy mean value theorem, $C_j$ is increasing and concave on $[0,e_j^{(k)}]$.
          Since $C_j$ is constant on $[e_j^{(k)},\infty)$ and $C_j(0)=f_j^{(\ell+1)}\ge0$, it is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and concave on $[0,\infty)$.

          It remains to prove $f_j\le C_j(e_j)$.
          Since $\mathbb{E} R_j=j/k<1$, we have $f_j<1$.
          Moreover, \cref{lem:product-shortfall}\textup{(ii)} implies that $0\le e_j\le e_j^{(k)}$.
          Since $0=e_j^{(\ell+1)}<\cdots<e_j^{(k)}$, we can choose an integer $s$ with $\ell+1\le s<k$ such that $e_j^{(s)}\le e_j\le e_j^{(s+1)}$.
          Since $\ell+e_j^{(s)}=\Psi_\ell(s)$, \cref{fact:retained-shortfall}\textup{(ii)} and the explicit formula for $\Psi_\ell^{-1}$ imply $f_j\le Q_{\ell,s}(e_j)$, where
          \[
            Q_{\ell,s}(v)
            =1-(\ell+v)+s^{-1/(s-\ell)}(\ell+v)^{1+1/(s-\ell)}.
          \]
          On $[e_j^{(s)},e_j^{(s+1)}]$, this function is convex, since
          \[
            Q_{\ell,s}''(v)
            =\frac{s-\ell+1}{(s-\ell)^2}s^{-1/(s-\ell)}(\ell+v)^{1/(s-\ell)-1}>0.
          \]

          By \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(i)} and the definition of $C_j$, for $t=s,s+1$, we have $Q_{\ell,s}(e_j^{(t)})=f_j^{(t)}=C_j(e_j^{(t)})$.
          Thus, $C_j$ is the chord joining the endpoint values of the convex function $Q_{\ell,s}$ on $[e_j^{(s)},e_j^{(s+1)}]$, so $Q_{\ell,s}(v)\le C_j(v)$ throughout this interval.
          Taking $v=e_j$, we obtain $f_j\le Q_{\ell,s}(e_j)\le C_j(e_j)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{le:allocation}\label{lem:allocation}
          Let $0\le\kappa_1\le\cdots\le\kappa_{k-1}$ and $w\ge0$.
          Suppose that the nonnegative numbers $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ and $f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1}$ satisfy $e_1=0$, $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$ for $1\le j<k$, $f_j\le C_j(e_j)$ for $1\le j<k$, and $e_k\le w$.
          Then
          \[
            \sum_{j<k}\kappa_jf_j
            \le
            \begin{cases}
              \displaystyle\sum_{j<k}\kappa_jf_j^*(w),
               & 0\le w\le W_k, \\[4pt]
              \displaystyle\sum_{j<k}\kappa_jf_j^{(k)},
               & w>W_k.
            \end{cases}
          \]
          For $0\le w\le W_k$, equality holds when $e_j=e_j^*(w)$ and $f_j=f_j^*(w)$.
          For $w>W_k$, equality holds when $e_j=e_j^{(k)}$ and $f_j=f_j^{(k)}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
For $w>W_k$, the monotonicity of $C_j$ and the definition of $C_j$ imply $C_j(u)\le f_j^{(k)}$ for every $u\ge0$.
          Thus, $f_j\le f_j^{(k)}$ for each $j<k$, and summing with the nonnegative weights $\kappa_j$ yields $\sum_{j<k}\kappa_jf_j\le\sum_{j<k}\kappa_jf_j^{(k)}$.
          Equality holds when $e_j=e_j^{(k)}$ for $1\le j\le k$ and $f_j=f_j^{(k)}$ for $1\le j<k$.
          Indeed, \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(i)} gives $e_1=0$ and $e_{j+1}=e_j+f_j$, while the definition of $C_j$ gives $f_j=C_j(e_j)$ for $j<k$, with $e_k=W_k<w$.

          Now suppose that $0\le w\le W_k$ and choose $1\le s<k$ with $W_s\le w\le W_{s+1}$.
          We first verify that the bound in \cref{lem:allocation} is attained when $e_j=e_j^*(w)$ for $1\le j\le k$ and $f_j=f_j^*(w)$ for $1\le j<k$.
          For $1\le j<k$, the numbers $e_j^*(w)$ and $f_j^*(w)$ are nonnegative by the definitions of $e_j^*$ and $f_j^*$.
          We have $e_1^*(w)=0$, $e_{j+1}^*(w)=e_j^*(w)+f_j^*(w)$, and $e_k^*(w)=w$ by \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(ii)}.
          For $j<k-s$, both $e_j^*(w)$ and $f_j^*(w)$ are zero.
          At $j=k-s$, we have $e_j^*(w)=0$ and $0\le f_j^*(w)\le C_j(0)$.
          For $k-s<j<k$, substituting $e_j^*(w)$ from the definitions of $e_j^*$ and $f_j^*$ into the definition of $C_j$, we obtain $C_j(e_j^*(w))=f_j^*(w)$.
          Thus, all the hypotheses of \cref{lem:allocation} hold with $e_j=e_j^*(w)$ for $1\le j\le k$ and $f_j=f_j^*(w)$ for $1\le j<k$.
          The corresponding weighted sum is $\sum_{j<k}\kappa_jf_j^*(w)$.

          For arbitrary nonnegative numbers $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ and $f_1,\ldots,f_{k-1}$ satisfying the hypotheses of \cref{lem:allocation}, it remains to prove
          \[
            \sum_{j<k}\kappa_j(f_j-f_j^*(w))\le0.
          \]
          Set $d_j=e_j-e_j^*(w)$ and $g_j=f_j-f_j^*(w)$.
          Subtracting the equalities in \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(ii)} from the assumed inequalities $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$, we find $d_{j+1}\ge d_j+g_j$, while $d_k=e_k-w\le0$.
          We first bound the terms through $j=k-s$ in terms of $d_{k-s+1}$.

          Since $f_j^*(w)=0$ for $j<k-s$, $e_{k-s+1}^*(w)=f_{k-s}^*(w)$, and the weights are nondecreasing, summing the assumed inequalities $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$ yields
          \begin{equation}\label{eq:sec3-allocation-initial}
            \begin{aligned}
              \sum_{j\le k-s}\kappa_jg_j
               & \le\kappa_{k-s}\left(\sum_{j\le k-s}f_j-f_{k-s}^*(w)\right)\le\kappa_{k-s}(e_{k-s+1}-e_{k-s+1}^*(w)) \\
               & =\kappa_{k-s}d_{k-s+1}.
            \end{aligned}
          \end{equation}
          For $k-s<j<k$, let $\alpha_j$ be the slope of the segment of $C_j$ joining nodes $s$ and $s+1$, that is, $\alpha_j=\frac{f_j^{(s+1)}-f_j^{(s)}}{e_j^{(s+1)}-e_j^{(s)}}$.
          By the concavity of $C_j$ and $f_j^*(w)=C_j(e_j^*(w))$,
          \[
            g_j\le C_j(e_j)-C_j(e_j^*(w))\le\alpha_jd_j.
          \]
          Set $\Gamma_{k-s}=\kappa_{k-s}$ and $\Gamma_j=(\Gamma_{j-1}+\kappa_j\alpha_j)/(1+\alpha_j)$ for $k-s<j<k$.
          Since $0\le\Gamma_{j-1}\le\kappa_{j-1}\le\kappa_j$, induction shows that $0\le\Gamma_j\le\kappa_j$.
          By the definition of $\Gamma_j$, we obtain
          \[
            \Gamma_{j-1}d_j+\kappa_jg_j =\Gamma_j(d_j+g_j)
            +(\kappa_j-\Gamma_j)(g_j-\alpha_jd_j)\le\Gamma_jd_{j+1}.
          \]
          Applying the preceding inequality repeatedly for $k-s<j<k$ and using \eqref{eq:sec3-allocation-initial}, we obtain
          \[
            \sum_{j<k}\kappa_jg_j
            \le\Gamma_{k-s}d_{k-s+1}+\sum_{k-s<j<k}\kappa_jg_j
            \le\Gamma_{k-1}d_k\le0.
          \]
          This proves the asserted maximum on $[W_s,W_{s+1}]$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:critical}
          Let $k\ge2$, and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ be independent with a common law $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ of mean $1/k$.
          Set $R_k=\sum_{i=1}^kY_i$, $f_k=\mathbb{P}(R_k\ge1)$, and $w=e_k=k\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+$.
          Then the following statements hold.
          \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
            \item\label{it:critical-tail} We have $0\le w=e_k\le W_k$ and $1-f_k\ge H(w)$.
            \item\label{it:critical-shape} The function $H$ is continuous on $[0,W_k]$, satisfies $H(W_s)=(1-1/s)^s$ for $1\le s\le k$, and is strictly concave on each $[W_s,W_{s+1}]$ with $1\le s<k$.
          \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:product-shortfall}\textup{(ii)} with $j=k$, we have $0\le w\le W_k$.
          We next prove $1-f_k\ge H(w)$.
          If $w=0$, then $H(w)=0\le1-f_k$ as desired.
          If $w>0$, then $\mathbb{E} R_k=1$ implies $\mathbb{E}(1-R_k)_+=w/k>0$, so $f_k<1$.
          Applying \cref{fact:retained-shortfall}\textup{(ii)} with $j=k$ and $\ell=0$, we obtain $1-f_k\ge w/\Psi_0^{-1}(w)=H(w)$.

          The function $H$ is continuous on $[0,W_k]$ and satisfies $H(W_s)=(1-1/s)^s$ for $1\le s\le k$.
          For each integer $s$ with $1\le s<k$, the function $H$ is strictly concave on $[W_s,W_{s+1}]$, since
          \[
            H''(u)=-(s+1)s^{-2-1/s}u^{1/s-1}<0
          \]
          for every $u\in(W_s,W_{s+1})$.
          This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:strict-chord}
          Let $k\ge2$ and $0<x<1/k$.
          Let $\mathsf P=(1-kx)\delta_0+kx\mathsf Q$, where $\mathsf Q$ is a probability distribution on $[0,1]$ with mean $1/k$.
          Suppose that $(1-a)/a\le2/(k-1)$.
          Then
          \[
            a^{-k}F_k(\mathsf P)\le1-H(w)+A(w).
          \]
          Moreover, if $W_s\le w\le W_{s+1}$ for an integer $1\le s<k$, then
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              1-H(w)+A(w)
               & \le(1-\theta)\bigl[1-H(W_s)+A(W_s)\bigr]         \\
               & \quad+\theta\bigl[1-H(W_{s+1})+A(W_{s+1})\bigr],
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          where $\theta=(w-W_s)/(W_{s+1}-W_s)$.
          The second inequality is strict when $W_s<w<W_{s+1}$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
We first check that $b_1\le\cdots\le b_{k-1}$, as required by \cref{lem:allocation}.
          If $k\ge3$ and $1\le j\le k-2$, then by the definition of $b_j$ we have
          \[
            \frac{b_{j+1}}{b_j}
            =\frac{(k-j)a}{(j+1)(1-a)}
            \ge\frac{2a}{(k-1)(1-a)}
            \ge1,
          \]
          since $k-j\ge2$, $j+1\le k-1$, and $(1-a)/a\le2/(k-1)$.
          For $k=2$, the sequence consists only of $b_1$.
          Thus, $b_1\le\cdots\le b_{k-1}$ holds for all $k$.

          By \cref{lem:allocation}, $\sum_{j<k}b_jf_j\le A(w)$, while by \cref{lem:critical} we have $f_k\le1-H(w)$.
          Substitution into \cref{fact:retained-sums}\textup{(i)} proves the first inequality.
          For the second inequality, fix any integer $s$ with $1\le s<k$ and $W_s\le w\le W_{s+1}$, and set $\theta=(w-W_s)/(W_{s+1}-W_s)$.
          Then $w=(1-\theta)W_s+\theta W_{s+1}$ and $0\le\theta\le1$.
          The function $A$ is affine on $[W_s,W_{s+1}]$ by definition, while $H$ is strictly concave there by \cref{lem:critical}\textup{(ii)}.
          Hence,
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              1-H(w)+A(w)
               & =1-H(w)+(1-\theta)A(W_s)
              +\theta A(W_{s+1})                         \\
               & \le1-(1-\theta)H(W_s)-\theta H(W_{s+1})
              +(1-\theta)A(W_s)
              +\theta A(W_{s+1})                         \\
               & =(1-\theta)\bigl[1-H(W_s)+A(W_s)\bigr]
              +\theta\bigl[1-H(W_{s+1})+A(W_{s+1})\bigr].
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          The inequality in the second line is strict when $0<\theta<1$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:crossing-upper}
          Let $k\ge5$ and set $\gamma=-\log(1-\mathrm{e}^{-1})$.
          Then
          \[
            c_k<\gamma+\frac{41}{500k}<\frac{11467}{25000}+\frac{41}{500k}.
          \]
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:initial-nodes}
          Let $k\ge2$ and $x=\beta_k$.
          \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
            \item For every integer $s$ with $2\le s\le\min\{4,k-1\}$, we have $A(W_s)<H(W_s)=((s-1)/s)^s$.
            \item We have $A(W_1)=H(W_1)=0$ and $A(W_k)=H(W_k)=(1-1/k)^k$.
                  \item\label{it:initial-fourth-gap} For $k\ge5$, we have
                  \[
                    H(W_4)-A(W_4)>\frac3{5000}-\frac1{400k}.
                  \]
            \item If $2\le k\le5$, then every nonnegative Borel law $\mathsf P$ maximizing $F_k$ under $m(\mathsf P)\le x$ has $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
                  If $k\ge6$, then every nonnegative Borel law $\mathsf P$ maximizing $F_k$ under $m(\mathsf P)\le x$ has $w=0$ or $W_4<w\le W_k$.
          \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
We first prove $c>\gamma>5/12$, where $\gamma=-\log(1-\mathrm{e}^{-1})$.
          Since $k\ge2$, we have $0<1-1/k<1$.
          By the definition of $g_k$, we have
          \[
            g_k(\gamma)
            =\int_0^1\left(1+\frac{\gamma-u}{k}\right)^{k-1}\,\mathrm{d} u
            <\int_0^1\mathrm{e}^{(1-1/k)(\gamma-u)}\,\mathrm{d} u
            \le\left(\int_0^1\mathrm{e}^{\gamma-u}\,\mathrm{d} u\right)^{1-1/k}=1.
          \]
          The first inequality follows from $\log(1+v)\le v$ for $v>-1$, with strict inequality in the integrands whenever $u\ne\gamma$.
          The second inequality follows from the concavity of $y\mapsto y^{1-1/k}$.
          Thus, $c>\gamma$ by the strict monotonicity of $g_k$.
          Since $\mathrm{e}<11/4$, we also have $\gamma>\mathrm{e}^{-1}+\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{-2}>52/121>5/12$.

          By the definitions of $e_j^*$ and $f_j^*$, we have $f_j^*(W_s)=f_j^{(s)}$ at every node $W_s$.
          Also, the definition of $b_j$ and $(1-a)/a=c/k$ imply $b_j=\binom{k}{j}(c/k)^{k-j}$.
          Substituting the values of $f_j^{(s)}$ from \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(i)} into the definition of $A$, we obtain
          \[
            A(W_s)
            =\sum_{h=1}^{s-1}\binom{k}{h}\left(\frac ck\right)^h
            \left[1-\left(1-\frac1s\right)^{s-h}\right]
            \qquad(1\le s\le k).
          \]
          Taking $s=1$, we obtain $A(W_1)=H(W_1)=0$.
          For $s=k$, by separating the two terms in the summand and applying the binomial theorem, we have
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              A(W_k)
               & =\left(1+\frac ck\right)^k
              -\left(1+\frac{c-1}{k}\right)^k-1+\left(1-\frac1k\right)^k \\
               & =g_k(c)-1+\left(1-\frac1k\right)^k=H(W_k),
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          where we used $g_k(c)=1$.
          For $2\le s\le\min\{4,k\}$, define $Q_s=A(W_s)/H(W_s)$.
          To prove \textup{(i)}, we must show that $Q_s<1$ for $2\le s\le\min\{4,k-1\}$.
          Evaluating the sum for $A(W_s)$ at $s=2,3,4$ with $s\le k$ and dividing by $H(W_s)=(1-1/s)^s$, we obtain
          \begin{equation}\label{eq:sec3-initial-node-values}
            \begin{aligned}
              Q_2 & =2c,                                     \\
              Q_3 & =\frac{15c}{8}+\frac{9(1-1/k)c^2}{16},   \\
              Q_4 & =\frac{148c}{81}+\frac{56(1-1/k)c^2}{81}
              +\frac{32(1-1/k)(1-2/k)c^3}{243},
            \end{aligned}
          \end{equation}
          and hence
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              Q_3-Q_2
               & =\frac{c}{16}\bigl(9(1-1/k)c-2\bigr) &          & (k\ge3), \\
              Q_4-Q_3
               & =\frac{c}{3888}
              \bigl(501(1-1/k)c+512(1-1/k)(1-2/k)c^2-186\bigr)
               &                                      & (k\ge4).
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          For $k\ge3$, the bounds $c>5/12$ and $1-1/k\ge2/3$ imply $Q_3-Q_2>c/32>0$.
          For $k\ge4$, using $c>5/12$, $1-1/k\ge3/4$, and $1-2/k\ge1/2$, we obtain $Q_4-Q_3>(c/3888)(187/48)>0$.
          When $k=2$, there is no integer $s$ with $2\le s<k$.
          Since $A(W_k)=H(W_k)$, we have $Q_2<Q_3=1$ when $k=3$ and $Q_2<Q_3<Q_4=1$ when $k=4$.
          Thus, \textup{(i)} holds for $2\le k\le4$.

          For $k\ge5$, the inequalities $Q_2<Q_3<Q_4$ show that it suffices to prove $Q_4<1$.
          We prove the stronger bound in \textup{(iii)}.

          Set $C=41/500$ and $c_+(u)=11467/25000+Cu$ for $0\le u\le1/5$.
          Define
          \begin{equation}\label{eq:sec3-fourth-comparison-function}
            R(u)=\frac{37c_+(u)}{64}+\frac{7(1-u)c_+(u)^2}{32}
            +\frac{(1-u)(1-2u)c_+(u)^3}{24}.
          \end{equation}
          By \cref{lem:crossing-upper}, $c<c_+(1/k)$ for $k\ge5$.
          Since the expression for $Q_4$ in \eqref{eq:sec3-initial-node-values} is strictly increasing in $c\ge0$ and $H(W_4)=81/256$, we obtain $A(W_4)<R(1/k)$.
          On $[0,1/5]$, we have $5/12<c_+(u)<1/2$.
          Differentiating \eqref{eq:sec3-fourth-comparison-function} and using $5/12<c_+(u)<1/2$ and $0\le u\le1/5$, we obtain
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              R''(u)
               & =-\frac{7Cc_+(u)}8+\frac{7C^2(1-u)}{16}
              +\frac{c_+(u)^3}{6}-\frac{C(3-4u)c_+(u)^2}{4}
              +\frac{C^2(1-u)(1-2u)c_+(u)}4                       \\
               & \le-\frac{35C}{96}+\frac{9C^2}{16}+\frac1{48}<0.
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          Direct calculation shows that $R(1/5)<81/256-1/10000$ and $R'(1/5)>1/400$.
          Since $R''<0$ on $[0,1/5]$, we have $R'(u)\ge R'(1/5)>1/400$ throughout this interval.
          For $k\ge5$, using $A(W_4)<R(1/k)$ and integrating $R'$ over $[1/k,1/5]$, we obtain
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              H(W_4)-A(W_4)
               & >\frac{81}{256}-R(1/k)                            \\
               & =\frac{81}{256}-R(1/5)+\int_{1/k}^{1/5}R'(u)\,\mathrm{d} u \\
               & \ge\frac{81}{256}-R(1/5)+R'(1/5)(1/5-1/k)         \\
               & >\frac1{10000}+\frac{1/5-1/k}{400}
              =\frac3{5000}-\frac1{400k}>0.
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          This proves \cref{lem:initial-nodes}\textup{(iii)} and $Q_4<1$.
          The inequalities $Q_2<Q_3<Q_4$ now imply $A(W_s)<H(W_s)$ for $s=2,3,4$ when $k\ge5$.

          Finally, let $\mathsf P$ be any law maximizing $F_k$ among laws with mean at most $\beta_k$.
          By \cref{prop:normalization}, we may write $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$, where $a=k\beta_k$ and $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$.
          By \cref{lem:critical}, $0\le w\le W_k$.
          By \cref{lem:crossing-parameters}, $(1-a)/a=c/k\le1/(2k)<2/(k-1)$, so \cref{prop:strict-chord} applies.
          Since $\mathsf B_{\beta_k}$ has mean $\beta_k$ and attains $F_k(\mathsf B_{\beta_k})=a^k$, maximality and \cref{prop:strict-chord} imply
          \[
            1\le a^{-k}F_k(\mathsf P)\le1-H(w)+A(w),
          \]
          and hence $H(w)-A(w)\le0$.
          The difference $H-A$ is zero at $W_1=0$ and $W_k$, and positive at $W_s$ for $2\le s\le\min\{4,k-1\}$.
          Fix any integer $s$ with $1\le s<k$ such that $H(W_s)\ge A(W_s)$ and $H(W_{s+1})\ge A(W_{s+1})$.
          By \cref{lem:critical}\textup{(ii)} and the definitions of $e_j^*$ and $f_j^*$ and $A$, for every $u\in(W_s,W_{s+1})$ we have
          \[
            \begin{aligned}
              H(u)
               & >\frac{W_{s+1}-u}{W_{s+1}-W_s}H(W_s)
              +\frac{u-W_s}{W_{s+1}-W_s}H(W_{s+1})      \\
               & \ge\frac{W_{s+1}-u}{W_{s+1}-W_s}A(W_s)
              +\frac{u-W_s}{W_{s+1}-W_s}A(W_{s+1})
              =A(u).
            \end{aligned}
          \]
          For $2\le k\le5$, this proves $H(u)-A(u)>0$ for every $0<u<W_k$.
          Since $0\le w\le W_k$ and $H(w)-A(w)\le0$, we have $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
          For $k\ge6$, the same argument excludes $0<w\le W_4$, leaving $w=0$ or $W_4<w\le W_k$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:low-dimensional-crossing}
          Let $2\le k\le5$.
          For every nonnegative Borel law $\mathsf P$ of mean at most $\beta_k$, $F_k(\mathsf P)\le(k\beta_k)^k=1-(1-\beta_k)^k$.
          Moreover, every maximizing law has $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf P$ be any maximizing law under the mean bound $\beta_k$.
          Such a law exists by \cref{lem:attainment}.
          By \cref{prop:normalization}, $\mathsf P$ has mean $\beta_k$ and has the form $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$ with $a=k\beta_k$ and $m(\mathsf Q)=1/k$.
          Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ be independent with law $\mathsf Q$ and set $w=k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+$.
          By \cref{lem:initial-nodes}, $w=0$ or $w=W_k$.
          By \cref{lem:crossing-parameters}, $(1-a)/a=c_k/k\le1/(2k)<2/(k-1)$, so \cref{prop:strict-chord} applies and gives
          \[
            a^{-k}F_k(\mathsf P)\le1-H(w)+A(w)=1,
          \]
          where the equality follows from \cref{lem:initial-nodes}\textup{(ii)} at $w=0,W_k$.
          Both candidate laws attain $(k\beta_k)^k$, proving the maximum.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:remaining-excess-range}
          Let $k\ge6$ and let $\mathsf P$ be a maximizing law with $m(\mathsf P)\le \beta_k$.
          Write $\mathsf P=(1-k\beta_k)\delta_0+k\beta_k\mathsf Q$ as in \cref{prop:normalization}, and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ be independent with law $\mathsf Q$.
          If $w=k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+$ satisfies $0<w<W_k$, then $W_4<w<W_k$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:initial-nodes}\textup{(iv)}, we have $W_4<w<W_k$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- observation-1: body_md -->
\label{obs:contact-identities}
  Let $k\ge6$ and $0<x<1/k$, and suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel probability laws of mean at most $x$.
  With $h,p,M,D$ as defined above, the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:contact-majorant}\label{item:contact-equality}
    For every $z\in[0,1]$,
    \[
      h(z)\le F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)
      +\frac{F_k(\mathsf P)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)}x z,
    \]
    with equality for $\mathsf P$-almost every $z$.

    \item\label{item:contact-failure} We have $x<M\le1$ and $\mathsf P([0,M])=1$.
    Moreover, for $\mathsf P$-almost every $z$,
    \[
      1-h(z)=\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-z)=\frac{p(M-z)}D.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end observation-1 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The upper bound in \ref{item:contact-majorant} follows from \eqref{eq:contact-first-variation}.
  Since $\int z\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P(z)=x$ and $\int h\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P=F_k(\mathsf P)$, we have
  \[
    \int\left(
    F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)
    +\frac{F_k(\mathsf P)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)}x z-h(z)
    \right)\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P(z)=0.
  \]
  The integrand is nonnegative by \ref{item:contact-majorant}, so it vanishes $\mathsf P$-almost everywhere.
  This proves the equality assertion in \ref{item:contact-equality}.

  We have $M>x$ because $D>0$.
  Taking $z=1$ in \ref{item:contact-majorant} shows that $M\le1$.
  Also, the definitions imply $p/D=(F_k(\mathsf P)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P))/x$ and $1-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)=pM/D$.
  By \ref{item:contact-equality}, for $\mathsf P$-almost every $z$,
  we have
  $h(z)=F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)+(F_k(\mathsf P)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P))z/x
    =F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)+pz/D$.
  Using $1-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)=pM/D$, we obtain
  $1-h(z)=pM/D-pz/D=p(M-z)/D$.
  Since $1-h(z)=\mathbb{P}(S_{k-1}<1-z)$, this proves the formula
  in \ref{item:contact-failure}.
  Since its left-hand side is nonnegative and $p/D>0$, we have $z\le M$ for $\mathsf P$-almost every $z$.
  Hence, $\mathsf P([0,M])=1$, proving \ref{item:contact-failure}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:contact-moments}
  Let $k\ge6$ and $0<x<1/k$, and suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel probability laws of mean at most $x$.
  With $p,r,M,D,\delta,B$ as defined above, the following statements hold.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:contact-moment-identity} We have $B>0$ and
    $
      \operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\frac{DB}{k}\text{ and }
      \operatorname{Var}(S_k)=DB=(M-x)(r-\delta).
    $
    \item\label{item:contact-excess-identities} We have
    $
      pr=\delta+\mathbb{E}(S_k-1)_+
      \text{ and }1-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)=\frac{pM}{M-x}.
    $
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The event $S_k<1$ is unchanged by permuting the coordinates, so $\mathbb{E}[X_1\mid S_k<1]=(1-r)/k$.
  Taking $\varphi(z)=z$ in \eqref{eq:conditional-reweighting}, we obtain
  \[
    \frac{1-r}{k}=\frac{Mx-\mathbb{E} X_1^2}{D}
    =x-\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X_1)}D.
  \]
  Subtracting $(1-r)/k$ from $x$ in the last equality and multiplying by $D>0$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \operatorname{Var}(X_1)
       & =D\left(x-\frac{1-r}{k}\right)
      =\frac Dk(kx-1+r)                 \\
       & =\frac Dk(r-\delta)
      =\frac{DB}{k},
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  where we used $\delta=1-kx$ and $B=r-\delta$.
  The variables $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ are independent and have the same variance, so
  \[
    \operatorname{Var}(S_k)=\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{Var}(X_i)
    =k\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=DB=(M-x)(r-\delta).
  \]
  Since $x>0$ and $\mathsf P(\{0\})>0$, the law is nonconstant.
  Thus, $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)>0$, and $D>0$ implies $B>0$.
  This proves \ref{item:contact-moment-identity}.

  Taking expectations in $(1-S_k)_+-(S_k-1)_+=1-S_k$ and using $\mathbb{E}(1-S_k)_+=pr$ and $\mathbb{E} S_k=1-\delta$ proves the first equality in \ref{item:contact-excess-identities}.
  The second follows from the definitions of $M$ and $D$.
  This proves \ref{item:contact-excess-identities}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:contact-moment}
  Let $k\ge6$ and $0<x<1/k$, and suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel probability laws of mean at most $x$.
    {Use the notation above.}
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:contact-moment-formula} For independent $X,X'\sim\mathsf P$, we have
    \[
      B(M-r)=v+\frac{k}{2p}\mathbb{E}\left[(X-X')
      \int_{X'}^X(h(t)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P))\,\mathrm{d} t\right].
    \]
    \item\label{item:contact-moment-bounds} We have $v\le B(M-r)$, $r\le M$, and
    \[
      \frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_k\mid S_k<1)}{\operatorname{Var}(S_k)}
      \le\frac{M-r}{M-x}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $T=S_k-X_1$ and $Q(z)=\mathbb{E}(1-T-z)_+$.
  Since $T$ is independent of $X_1$, we have $Q(X_1)=\mathbb{E}[(1-S_k)_+\mid X_1]$.
  Symmetry and $S_k-kx=\delta-(1-S_k)$ give
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      \operatorname{Cov}(X_1,Q(X_1))
       & =\frac1k\mathbb{E}[(S_k-kx)(1-S_k)_+] \\
       & =\frac pk(\delta r-r^2-v)
      =-\frac pk(v+rB).
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  By Fubini's theorem, $Q(z)-Q(z')=-\int_{z'}^z(1-h(t))\,\mathrm{d} t$.
  For independent $X,X'\sim\mathsf P$, we have $2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Q(X))=\mathbb{E}[(X-X')(Q(X)-Q(X'))]$.
  Using $1-h(0)=pM/D$ and $\mathbb{E}(X-X')^2=2DB/k$ from {\cref{cor:contact-moments}\textup{\ref{item:contact-excess-identities}} and \textup{\ref{item:contact-moment-identity}}, respectively}, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      -\frac pk(v+rB)
       & =-\frac12\mathbb{E}\left[(X-X')\int_{X'}^X(1-h(t))\,\mathrm{d} t\right] \\
       & =-\frac{pMB}{k}
      +\frac12\mathbb{E}\left[(X-X')\int_{X'}^X(h(t)-h(0))\,\mathrm{d} t\right].
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Rearranging and using $h(0)=F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)$ proves \ref{item:contact-moment-formula}.
  Since $h(t)\ge h(0)$ for $t\ge0$, we have $(X-X')\int_{X'}^X(h(t)-h(0))\,\mathrm{d} t\ge0$.
  Thus, $v\le B(M-r)$, and $r\le M$ follows from $v\ge0$ and $B>0$.
  Since $D>0$, division by $\operatorname{Var}(S_k)=DB$ gives $v/\operatorname{Var}(S_k)\le(M-r)/D$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite-shortfall-margin}
  Let $k\ge6$ and $x=\beta_k$.
  Suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among Borel probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ of mean at most $x$.
  Assume $0<w<W_k$, with $w=k\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+$ as in \cref{sec:common-bounds}.
  Use $M$, $D$ and $r$ from \cref{sec:contact}.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:shortfall-margin} We have
    \[
      0\le M-r<\frac{M-x}{20}-\frac{3x}{20}.
    \]
    \item\label{item:shortfall-ratio} We have $D>3x$ and
    \[
      0\le\frac{M-r}{D}<\frac1{20}-\frac{3x}{20D}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:coupled-energy}
  Let $k\ge6$, $0<a<1$, and $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$, where $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$.
  For independent $Y_i\sim\mathsf Q$, set $w=k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+\in[0,W_k]$.
  Use the weights $v_j$ and the functions $E_*$ and $V_*$ defined above, and suppose that $v_1\le\cdots\le v_{k-1}$.
  For independent $X_i\sim\mathsf P$, write $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kX_i$.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:coupled-profile-general} We have $F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)\le V_*(w)$.
    \item\label{item:coupled-energy-bound} Suppose in addition that $w\in[W_4,W_k)$, let $s$ satisfy $4\le s<k$ and $W_s\le w<W_{s+1}$, and use $L(w)$ and $\Gamma_j$ defined above.
    If $\Gamma_j\ge0$ for every $k-s\le j<k$, then
    \[
      \mathbb{E}(S_k-1)_+-L(w)F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)\ge E_*(w)-L(w)V_*(w).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
By \cref{fact:retained-sums} with $x=a/k$, we have $F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)=\sum_{j<k}v_jf_j$ and $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$.
  Together with $f_j\le C_j(e_j)$ from \cref{lem:capacities}, these conditions allow us to apply \cref{lem:allocation} with weights $v_j$ and obtain $F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)\le\sum_{j<k}v_jf_j^*(w)=V_*(w)$.
  This proves \ref{item:coupled-profile-general}.
  We now assume the additional hypotheses of \ref{item:coupled-energy-bound}.
  Set $d_j=e_j-e_j^*(w)$ for $1\le j\le k$, and $g_j=f_j-f_j^*(w)$ for $1\le j<k$.
  By \cref{fact:retained-sums}\textup{(ii)}, we have
  $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$ for $1\le j<k$.
  By \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}\textup{(ii)}, we have
  $e_{j+1}^*(w)=e_j^*(w)+f_j^*(w)$.
  Subtracting this equality from $e_{j+1}\ge e_j+f_j$,
  we obtain
  $d_{j+1}=e_{j+1}-e_{j+1}^*(w)
    \ge(e_j-e_j^*(w))+(f_j-f_j^*(w))
    =d_j+g_j$.
  Moreover, $d_k=0$, since
  $e_k=e_k^*(w)=w$.
  For $k-s<j<k$, \cref{lem:capacities} gives that $C_j$ is concave and satisfies $f_j\le C_j(e_j)$.
  Also, $f_j^*(w)=C_j(e_j^*(w))$ by the definition of $C_j$ and  \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}.
  The function $C_j$ is affine with slope $\alpha_j$ on $[e_j^{(s)},e_j^{(s+1)}]$, which contains $e_j^*(w)$.
  Hence, by concavity,
  \[
    g_j\le C_j(e_j)-C_j(e_j^*(w))\le\alpha_jd_j.
  \]

  By \cref{fact:retained-sums}\textup{(i)} and the definitions of $E_*$ and $V_*$, the inequality
  \[
    \mathbb{E}(S_k-1)_+-L(w)F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)\ge E_*(w)-L(w)V_*(w)
  \]
  is equivalent to $\sum_{j<k}(L(w)v_jg_j-a^kb_jd_j/k)\le0$.
  We first handle the indices $j\le k-s$.
  By \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}, we have $e_j^*(w)=0$ and hence $d_j\ge0$ for $j\le k-s$, and $f_j^*(w)=0$ for $j<k-s$.
  Also, $e_{k-s+1}^*(w)=f_{k-s}^*(w)$ by \cref{fact:comparison-arrays}.
  {Summing $e_{j+1}-e_j\ge f_j$ from \cref{fact:retained-sums}\textup{(ii)} over $1\le j\le k-s$ and using $e_1=0$, we obtain $\sum_{j\le k-s}f_j\le e_{k-s+1}$.}
  Using $v_j\le v_{k-s}$ for $j\le k-s$ and $\Gamma_{k-s}=L(w)v_{k-s}$, we obtain
  \[
    \sum_{j\le k-s}\left(L(w)v_jg_j-\frac{a^kb_j}{k}d_j\right)
    \le L(w)v_{k-s}\left(\sum_{j\le k-s}f_j-f_{k-s}^*(w)\right)
    \le\Gamma_{k-s} d_{k-s+1}.
  \]
  By hypothesis, $\Gamma_j\ge0$.
  To prove the upper bound $\Gamma_j\le L(w)v_j$, start with $\Gamma_{k-s}=L(w)v_{k-s}$.
  If $\Gamma_{j-1}\le L(w)v_{j-1}\le L(w)v_j$, then, by the definition of $\Gamma_j$,
  \[
    (1+\alpha_j)\Gamma_j
    =\Gamma_{j-1}-\frac{a^kb_j}{k}+L(w)v_j\alpha_j
    \le L(w)v_j(1+\alpha_j).
  \]
  Induction yields $0\le\Gamma_j\le L(w)v_j$ for every $k-s\le j<k$.
  For $k-s<j<k$, using $d_j+g_j\le d_{j+1}$, $g_j\le\alpha_jd_j$, and the definition of $\Gamma_j$, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      L(w)v_jg_j-\frac{a^kb_j}{k}d_j
       & =\Gamma_j(d_j+g_j)-\Gamma_{j-1}d_j
      +(L(w)v_j-\Gamma_j)(g_j-\alpha_jd_j)   \\
       & \le\Gamma_jd_{j+1}-\Gamma_{j-1}d_j.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  Summing over $k-s<j<k$, we obtain
  \[
    \sum_{k-s<j<k}\left(L(w)v_jg_j-\frac{a^kb_j}{k}d_j\right)
    \le\Gamma_{k-1}d_k-\Gamma_{k-s} d_{k-s+1}.
  \]
  Combining the estimates for $j\le k-s$ and $k-s<j<k$ and using $d_k=0$, we obtain $\sum_{j<k}(L(w)v_jg_j-a^kb_jd_j/k)\le0$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:coupled-multipliers}
  Let $k\ge6$ and $4\le s<k$ be integers, and suppose that $11/24<c<1/2$.
  Write $x=1/(k+c)$, $a=kx$, and $p_0=(1-x)^k$.
  Let $w\in[W_s,W_{s+1})$, set $r_b=x(s+c)H(W_s)/p_0$, and use $L$, $E_*$, $V_*$, and $\Gamma_j$ defined above.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:coupled-multipliers} We have $\Gamma_j>0$ for every $k-s\le j<k$.
    \item\label{item:coupled-ratio} We have $r_b>x$ and $L(w)x/(r_b-x)^2<9/10$.
    \item\label{item:coupled-comparison} Let $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$, where $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$, and suppose that $k\mathbb{E}(Y_1+\cdots+Y_k-1)_+=w$ for independent $Y_i\sim\mathsf Q$.
    For independent $X_i\sim\mathsf P$ and $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kX_i$, we have
    $
      F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)\le V_*(w)
    $
    and
    \[
      \mathbb{E}(S_k-1)_+-L(w)F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)
      \ge E_*(w)-L(w)V_*(w).
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:crossing-lower-finite}
  For every integer $k\ge6$, we have
  \[
    c_k>\frac{11}{24}+\frac{2}{25k}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:sec4-parameter-bounds}
  Let $k\ge6$ and $x=\beta_k$.
  Then
  \[
    \frac{11}{24}+\frac{2}{25k}<c<\frac{19}{40},\text{ }
    \frac{12}{13}<a<1\text{ and }\frac13<p_0<\mathrm{e}^{-1}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The bounds on $c$ follow from {\cref{lem:crossing-lower-finite,lem:crossing-upper}} and $k\ge6$.
  Since $0<c<1/2$, we have $1>a=k/(k+c)>k/(k+1/2)\ge12/13$.
  Since $c<1/2$, we have $p_0<((2k-1)/(2k+1))^k<\mathrm{e}^{-1}$.
  The lower bound $p_0>1/3$ follows from $p_0>(1-1/k)^k\ge(5/6)^6>1/3$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:node-shortfall-margin}
  Let $k\ge6$, $x=\beta_k$, $a=kx$, $\delta=1-a$, and $p_0=1-a^k=(1-x)^k$.
  Use the functions $E_*$ and $V_*$ defined in \cref{sec:sec3-energy-comparison}.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt]
    \item\label{item:profile-positive} For every $t\in[W_4,W_k]$, we have $V_*(t)<a^k$.
    \item\label{item:profile-margin} Define
    \[
      r_*(t)=\frac{\delta+E_*(t)}{p_0}\text{ and }
      M_*(t)=\frac{x(1-V_*(t))}{a^k-V_*(t)}
      =x+\frac{xp_0}{a^k-V_*(t)}.
    \]
    For every $t\in[W_4,W_k]$, we have
    \[
      r_*(t)-\frac{19M_*(t)}{20}>\frac{x}{5}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Recall that $a=kx$, $\delta=1-a$, and $p_0=1-a^k=(1-x)^k$.
  By \cref{prop:normalization}, write $\mathsf P=(1-a)\delta_0+a\mathsf Q$ with $m(\mathsf Q)=1/k$.
  We have $0<p\le p_0$ since $\mathbb{E} S_k=a<1$ and $F_k(\mathsf P)\ge a^k$ by maximality.
  By \cref{cor:remaining-excess-range}, $W_4<w<W_k$.
  Let $s$ be the unique integer with $4\le s<k$ and $W_s\le w<W_{s+1}$.
  Set $r_b=x(s+c)H(W_s)/p_0$, and write $r_*=r_*(w)$ and $M_*=M_*(w)$.

  We first show that $x<r_b\le r\le M\le M_*$.
  Recall that $X_i=I_iY_i$, where the $I_i$ are independent Bernoulli variables of mean $a$ and are independent of $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$.
  Thus, $\mathbb{E}[S_k\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_k]=aR_k$.
  Since $(1-S_k)_+\ge0$ and $(1-S_k)_+\ge1-S_k$, we have
  \[
    \mathbb{E}[(1-S_k)_+\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_k]\ge\max\{0,1-aR_k\}\ge a(1-R_k)_++\delta\1_{\{R_k<1\}}.
  \]
  The last inequality is an equality when $R_k<1$, while its right-hand side is zero when $R_k\ge1$.
  Since $\mathbb{E} R_k=km(\mathsf Q)=1$ and $e_k=w$, we have $\mathbb{E}(1-R_k)_+=\mathbb{E}(R_k-1)_+=w/k$.
  Taking expectations, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      pr=\mathbb{E}(1-S_k)_+
       & \ge\frac{aw}{k}+\delta\mathbb{P}(R_k<1) \\
       & =\frac{aw}{k}+\delta(1-f_k)        \\
       & \ge\frac{aw}{k}+\delta H(w).
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The last inequality uses $1-f_k\ge H(w)$ from \cref{lem:critical}.
  By concavity of $H$ on $[W_s,W_{s+1}]$, we have
  \[
    H(w)\ge\min\{H(W_s),H(W_{s+1})\}=H(W_s),
  \]
  where the equality uses $H(W_{s+1})\ge H(W_s)$.
  Using $w\ge W_s=sH(W_s)$, $a/k=x$, and $\delta=cx$, we obtain
  \[
    pr\ge x(s+c)H(W_s),
  \]
  and hence $r\ge r_b$, since $p\le p_0$.

  By {\cref{lem:contact-moment}}, $r\le M$.
  Also, {\cref{lem:coupled-multipliers}\textup{\ref{item:coupled-comparison}}}, {\cref{lem:node-shortfall-margin}\textup{\ref{item:profile-positive}}}, and $p\le p_0$ imply
  \[
    M=x+\frac{xp}{F_k(\mathsf P)-F_{k-1}(\mathsf P)}
    \le x+\frac{xp_0}{a^k-V_*(w)}=M_*.
  \]
  Together with {\cref{lem:coupled-multipliers}\textup{\ref{item:coupled-ratio}}}, this proves
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sec4-parameter-order}
    x<r_b\le r\le M\le M_*.
  \end{equation}

  Combining {\cref{lem:coupled-multipliers}\textup{\ref{item:coupled-comparison}}} and {\cref{cor:contact-moments}\textup{\ref{item:contact-excess-identities}}}, we obtain
  \[
    \begin{aligned}
      r+\frac{L(w)M}{M-x}
       & \ge\frac{\delta+E_*(w)+L(w)(1-V_*(w))}{p}   \\
       & \ge\frac{\delta+E_*(w)+L(w)(1-V_*(w))}{p_0}
      =r_*+\frac{L(w)M_*}{M_*-x}.
    \end{aligned}
  \]
  The second inequality uses $0<p\le p_0$ and $\delta+E_*(w)+L(w)(1-V_*(w))>0$.
  The last equality follows from the definitions of $r_*$ and $M_*$ in {\cref{lem:node-shortfall-margin}}.
  By {\cref{lem:coupled-multipliers}\textup{\ref{item:coupled-ratio}}} and {\eqref{eq:sec4-parameter-order}},
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sec4-parameter-loss}
    r_*-r
    \le\frac{L(w)x(M_*-M)}{(M-x)(M_*-x)}
    \le\frac9{10}(M_*-M).
  \end{equation}
  Combining {\eqref{eq:sec4-parameter-order}}, {\eqref{eq:sec4-parameter-loss}}, and {\cref{lem:node-shortfall-margin}\textup{\ref{item:profile-margin}}}, we obtain
  \[
    r-\frac{19M}{20}
    \ge r_*-\frac{19M_*}{20}+\frac{M_*-M}{20}
    >\frac{x}{5}.
  \]
  Rearranging and using $r\le M$ proves \ref{item:shortfall-margin}.
  Since $M-r\ge0$, the upper bound $M-r<(D-3x)/20$ implies $D>3x$.
  Dividing by $D$ proves \ref{item:shortfall-ratio}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:support-separation}
  Let $k\ge6$ be an integer and $x=\beta_k$.
  Suppose that $\mathsf P$ maximizes $F_k$ among nonnegative Borel probability laws of mean at most $x$.
  Write $\mathsf P=(1-kx)\delta_0+kx\mathsf Q$, where $\mathsf Q\in\mathcal{P}([0,1])$ has mean $1/k$.
